segments.start_exact:
When Charlie Shaw, the carefree cow-puncher, was accused of
    being a shallow josher, and therefore worthless for rounding
    up cow thieves, Charlie got angry and proved that even a
    "kidder" can get down to business.
segments.end_exact: Even a natural clown has his serious moments.

segments.start_exact:
In the morning, with his own matutinal coffee bestowed where it would do
the most good, and the grading crews stringing out to work in a cold
dawn, Charlie walked into the camp and sought the head cook.
segments.end_exact: Two scraggy cows a day? Hardly.
segments.summary: Charlie attempts to sell beef to the camp contractor, offering progressively lower prices. The contractor claims he can get it cheaper, confirming to Charlie that stolen beef is being purchased. Charlie then observes the small herd and realizes only two cows per day are being butchered for 400+ men, indicating the real beef comes from elsewhere.

gacd.goal: Determine whether the construction camp is buying stolen cattle at suspiciously low prices
gacd.action: Charlie negotiates with the camp contractor, offering beef at progressively lower prices (from 4 cents to 3 cents per pound)
gacd.conflict: The contractor resists, claiming he can get it cheaper, which contradicts legitimate market prices

segments.reason: Charlie pursues a specific goal with on-stage action (negotiation with the contractor) that meets resistance and yields a clear success: Charlie confirms his suspicion that the camp is purchasing stolen beef at prices far below market value. The math proves the discrepancy—two scraggy cows per day cannot feed 400+ men when prime beef from the meat house hangs from hooks.

grassy rise. Nothing like a wagon arrived or departed. When dusk fell
again, he packed his outfit and rode back to the construction camp.
segments.end_exact: To-morrow he would make Elmer sing a different tune.

segments.summary: Charlie is knocked unconscious and wrapped in a wet rawhide hide by the cattle rustlers. He escapes by pulling a concealed pistol from a Texas holster, shoots one rustler, subdues the other, and escorts his prisoner to the Seventy-seven ranch with the stolen beef wagon.

gacd.goal: Catch the cattle rustlers and recover the stolen beef
gacd.action: Charlie sneaks up on the corral with his carbine, but is ambushed and knocked unconscious. He revives, escapes from the rawhide bondage using a hidden six-shooter, kills one rustler, subdues and captures the other
gacd.conflict: Charlie is outnumbered, trapped, and nearly killed in an incinerator pit; he must fight his way out against the rustlers' intent to murder him

segments.reason: This segment demonstrates clear GACD structure: Charlie's goal is to catch the rustlers; his action is the assault on the corral (though it initially fails due to ambush); the conflict is severe (capture, attempted murder by immolation); the outcome is success (he escapes, kills one attacker, subdues and captures the other, recovers the stolen beef wagon). This is a dramatic_scene of high stakes action and reversal.

segments.start_exact:
Charlie lifted his head from a bunk in one corner of the Seventy-seven
ranch house. A wagon was clattering into the yard. Elmer Duffy and half
a dozen riders flanked it like a bodyguard.
segments.end_exact:
I was born in El Paso. I come up the trail when it was a tough
proposition. I'm twenty-six years old, an', by Judas priest, I ain't
never died a winter yet!
segments.summary: Charlie arrives at the Seventy-seven with the stolen beef wagon and his prisoner. Elmer Duffy acknowledges Charlie's success, offers him $500 reward and a permanent job, but Charlie proudly refuses both, insisting he did it to prove his point and declaring his independence and self-reliance.

erac.choice: Decides to refuse the money, job, and gratitude; chooses to leave on his own terms, asserting his independence and self-respect
